extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP practitioners and patent professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for how patent claims should be interpreted when assessing patentability under the EPC, based on EPO Enlarged Board of Appeal decision G1/24 and its harmonisation with UPC/national practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as starting point for patentability assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The starting point and basis for assessing patentability under Articles 52 to 57 EPC is the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBA referred to existing case law applying provisions analogously to examining patentability and extracted the principle that claims are the primary reference when assessing novelty, inventive step and other patentability requirements. This emphasises that claim language anchors the assessment even where other parts of the file are consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The description and any drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims, not just in cases of unclarity or ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBA rejected prior Board of Appeal case law that saw no need to refer to descriptions and drawings where a claim appeared clear in isolation. The decision aligns EPO practice with national courts and the UPC and stresses consulting the description/drawings as a mandatory step in claim interpretation for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 69(1) EPC and Protocol not a legal basis for patentability interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 69(1), second sentence, EPC and Article 1 of the Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 EPC, being only concerned with infringement actions, could not serve as legal basis for claim interpretation when assessing patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Article 69/Protocol inform claim interpretation in infringement contexts, the EBA holds they are not the legal foundation for interpretation in patentability (examination/opposition) proceedings; instead analogous case law and general principles are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC does not provide claim interpretation guidance for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC does not provide guidance on how to interpret claims, so it cannot serve as an alternative legal basis for claim interpretation in patentability assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBA expressly found Article 84 inadequate as a source of interpretative rules for assessing patentability, reinforcing reliance on established case law principles and the claims-as-starting-point approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting description is required but does not necessarily allow overriding clear claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA orders that the description should always be consulted to interpret the claims, but consulting the description does not necessarily mean using it to override otherwise clear claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators note the nuance: the decision mandates consultation of the description/drawings but leaves open the extent to which a clear claim may be modified by descriptive definitions. Practitioners should expect examiners and tribunals to consult the description but not automatically accept descriptive definitions that contradict clear claim wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonisation principle with downstream tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA underlined the importance of uniformly applying claim interpretation principles in granting patents as well as revocation and infringement proceedings, aligning EPO practice with national courts and the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision states it would be 'a most unattractive proposition that the EPO deliberately adopt a contrary practice to that of the tribunals that are downstream of its patents.' This supports convergence of interpretative practice across forums and may affect prosecution, opposition and litigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresolved question on disregarding description definitions (question 3 inadmissible)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA deemed the question of whether a definition in the description can be disregarded when interpreting claims to assess patentability inadmissible (considered encompassed by the second question), leaving this specific issue unanswered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the EBA did not answer whether explicit descriptive definitions can be ignored, practical uncertainty remains. Practitioners report situations where examiners refuse to adopt a description-provided definition if it is not in the claim; the decision may not settle that examiner/tribunal practice. Expect debate and continued attention to how tribunals treat explicit definitions in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of prior Board of Appeal practice that omits consultation where claim appears clear
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA rejected contrary BoA case law which held there was no need to refer to descriptions and drawings when interpreting a clear claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry emphasises the anti-pattern the EBA overturned: treating isolated claim language as sufficient without consulting the rest of the application. Practitioners should avoid relying on the idea that a claim read in isolation will be decisive; always ensure the description/drawings support the intended claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implication for prosecution and opposition strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because descriptions and drawings must be consulted, applicants and opponents should ensure definitions, embodiments and drawings are drafted and relied on consistently to support claim interpretation across granting, opposition and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps include placing clear definitions and embodiments in the description that support intended claim scope, and being prepared to argue how the description informs claim meaning without improperly broadening or contradicting clear claim text. The decision signals that harmonised downstream practice may influence how examiners and tribunals assess claim scope.
